title: A dusty welcome
caption: The Coalsack Nebula above an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A person's silhouette stands out against one of the Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, while the Coalsack Nebula appears as a dark smudge at the centre of the starry sky.

The telescope is one of four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes belonging to ESO's Very Large Telescope, alongside four giant 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes. Depending on each project's needs, the Auxiliary Telescopes can be moved along tracks to up to 30 observing positions. Working together as the VLT Interferometer, they combine the light they gather, letting researchers see the cosmos in great detail.

Of all the dark nebulae in the sky, the Coalsack is the most prominent. It is rich in dust, which absorbs and scatters most of the starlight behind it, so it appears as a dark smudge in the sky. Infrared light, however, passes through dust almost unhindered, so the hidden stars can be seen at those wavelengths. Dark clouds like this are more striking from the southern hemisphere than from the north.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at ESO's Paranal Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the star field around the dark Coalsack looks richer than it would to someone standing there.

explore: Many cultures see shapes in these dark clouds. The Mapuche people of Chile call the Coalsack pozoko, meaning 'water well'.
